newsitem.title: GREECE: OECD sees Greek inflation at 7.2 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees Greek inflation at 7.2 pct in 1997.

text.p: Greece's "hard drachma" policy will pull inflation down to an average 7.2 percent in 1997, but higher than projected real wage rises will slow disinflation and adversely affect employment and external competitiveness, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said.
The OECD forecasts the private consumption deflator at 7.2 percent on average in 1997 and 6.0 percent in 1998 from an expected 8.6 percent in 1996.

Consumer price inflation stood at 7.7 percent year-on-year in November. Central bank officials told Reuters they expected it to drop to at least 7.5 percent in December assuming the continuing farmers' blockade of road and rail links would not lead to price hikes.
The "hard drachma" policy aims at combating inflation by letting the drachma slide versus major euro currencies, mainly ecu, by much less than justified by inflation differentials.
The central bank has pre-announced a broadly stable ecu/drachma exchange rate for 1996 and it is expected to outline its foreign exchange policy for next year in the first two months of 1997.
The current account deficit is forecast at 3.5 percent of GDP in 1997 and 3.7 percent in 1998 from an expected 3.5 percent of GDP in 1996.

A combination of real exchange rate appreciation, divergent cyclical development between Greece and its major trading partners and a boom in investment good imports facilitated by easier foreign exchange borrowing from domestic firms accounted for the deficit's deterioration in 1996, it said.
On the fiscal front, the OECD report projected a "substantial move" towards tightening but said additional measures may be required to meet the ambitious 4.2 percent of GDP convergence plan target.

The report predicted a budget deficit of 5.7 percent of GDP in 1997 and 5.1 percent in 1998, but admitted it was difficult to quantify the yield from revenue and expenditure measures outlined in the 1997 budget.

"The overall yield from these measures as well as the effect on expenditure from the introduction of a new, more transparent, civil service wage structure is especially difficult to estimate," it said.

The 1996 budget deficit target of 7.6 percent of GDP would be difficult to meet despite a higher nominal GDP and any deviation would make the attainment of the 1997 budget target of 4.2 percent of GDP harder, it added.

The OECD predicted economic growth would pick up gradually, rising to 2.5 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998 from an expected 2.2 percent in 1996, fueled by a rise in business investment due to a high rate of return on capital, cheaper credit and the end of election-linked political uncertainty.
Greece's socialist government forecasts GDP growth at 2.6 percent of GDP against 2.0 percent in 1995. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
